title: Cheap First, Ask the LLM Later? Cost and Accuracy of Rule-Based, Native-PDF, and Text-Based LLM Extraction of Syllabus Deadlines
content: Students receive assessment deadlines inside course syllabi, usually as PDFs, and a growing number of tools use large language models (LLMs) to turn these documents into calendars. A common cost-saving design runs cheap rules first and calls the LLM only when the rules appear to fail. We test whether this saves money without losing accuracy. We compare five strategies on 16 public syllabi from eight institutions (151 hand-verified deadlines): regular-expression rules, a general-purpose date library, an LLM given the native PDF, an LLM given text extracted from the PDF, and a rule-first hybrid that calls the LLM only when the rules find fewer than three events. Each LLM strategy was run three times with gemini-3.1-flash-lite. The LLM strategies reached F1 scores of 0.708 (native PDF) and 0.657 (extracted text); the difference was not significant (p = 0.13), and the native-PDF input used fewer tokens with this model. The rule-first hybrid used 57.8% fewer tokens than the text-based LLM but lowered F1 to 0.370, a significant loss (p = 0.002). Rules alone scored 0.186, and 58% of their correctly placed month-day matches carried the wrong year. A sweep of the hybrid's routing threshold shows that every token saved cost accuracy. We release the code, labels, and all predictions.
